content: Rashes are changes in the color or texture of the skin. They can present in various forms and may be indicative of underlying conditions or external irritants. Symptoms of a Rash The cause of a rash can often be identified by its visible characteristics and associated symptoms. Causes of a Rash A simple rash is referred to as dermatitis, which means inflammation of the skin. Contact dermatitis occurs when the skin comes into contact with irritants such as: Chemicals in elastic, latex, and rubber products Cosmetics, soaps, and detergents Dyes and other chemicals in clothing Poison ivy, oak, or sumac Seborrheic dermatitis manifests as red, scaly patches around the eyebrows, eyelids, mouth, nose, trunk, and behind the ears. When it occurs on the scalp, it is called dandruff in adults and cradle cap in infants. Other common causes include: Eczema (atopic dermatitis): Often seen in individuals with allergies or asthma, presenting as red, itchy, and scaly skin. Psoriasis: Characterized by red, scaly, itchy patches, typically over joints and along the scalp. Fingernails may also be affected. Impetigo: A bacterial skin infection common in children, presenting as red sores that blister, ooze, and crust over. Shingles: A painful, blistering skin condition caused by the reactivation of the chickenpox virus, which can remain dormant for years. Childhood illnesses: Conditions such as chickenpox, measles, roseola, rubella, hand-foot-mouth disease, fifth disease, and scarlet fever. Medications and insect bites or stings. Certain medical conditions can also cause rashes, including: Lupus erythematosus Rheumatoid arthritis, particularly the juvenile type Kawasaki disease When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Call emergency services (911) if: You experience shortness of breath, throat tightness, or facial swelling. Your child develops a purple rash resembling a bruise. Contact your healthcare provider if: You have joint pain, fever, or a sore throat. You notice streaks of redness, swelling, or very tender areas, as these may indicate an infection. You are taking a new medication (do not stop or change medications without consulting your doctor). You suspect a tick bite. Home treatments are ineffective, or symptoms worsen. Treatment Options Most simple rashes improve with gentle skin care and avoiding irritants. General guidelines include: Avoid scrubbing the skin. Use minimal soap and opt for gentle cleansers. Avoid applying cosmetic lotions or ointments directly to the rash. Use warm (not hot) water for cleaning and pat the skin dry instead of rubbing. Discontinue any newly introduced cosmetics or lotions. Expose the affected area to air as much as possible. For poison ivy, oak, or sumac, calamine lotion may help. Hydrocortisone cream (1%) is available over the counter and can soothe many rashes. For eczema, apply moisturizers and consider oatmeal bath products to relieve symptoms. Psoriasis may require prescription treatments or ultraviolet (UV) light therapy. Seborrheic dermatitis can be managed by applying small amounts of anti-dandruff shampoo to affected areas, especially near hairlines, leaving it on for 10 minutes, and rinsing carefully. Discontinue use if irritation occurs. Impetigo typically requires antibacterial creams or oral antibiotics. Medical Evaluation Your doctor will perform a physical examination and ask about your medical history, medications, family health problems, recent illnesses, or exposures. Questions may include: When did the rash begin? What parts of the body are affected? Does anything improve or worsen the rash? Have you used any new soaps, detergents, lotions, or cosmetics recently? Have you been in wooded areas recently? Have you had any changes in medications? Have you noticed a tick or insect bite? Have you eaten anything unusual recently? Do you have other symptoms like itching or scaling? Do you have underlying medical conditions such as asthma or allergies? Tests may include: Allergy testing Blood tests Skin biopsy Skin scrapings Treatment depends on the cause and may involve medicated creams, oral medications, or skin surgery. While many primary care providers can manage common rashes, more complex skin disorders may require referral to a dermatologist. Prevention of Rashes Identify and avoid products that irritate your skin. If allergies are suspected, skin testing may be recommended. Ensure appropriate vaccinations for childhood illnesses, such as the varicella vaccine for chickenpox and the MMR vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella. Treat strep throat promptly to prevent scarlet fever. Wash hands frequently to prevent the spread of viruses like roseola, hand-foot-mouth disease, and fifth disease. Practice relaxation techniques such as yoga, meditation, or tai chi, as stress can exacerbate conditions like eczema, psoriasis, and seborrheic dermatitis.
